Feeling a little pessimistic for the game's future  
I've been playing since open beta. 600ish hours of play time and have spent a bit of money between the battle pass, monthly subs and then buying Stelle/Steam.

I obviously think it is a great game but right now I feel a bit pessimistic about the outlook and really wonder how much longer the game can sustainably run.

The following is just speculation but from everything we know this game was aiming to be somewhere on a comparable scale to Hearthstone, free to play with a massive player base contributing regular funds via cosmetic monetisation. "No plan survives contact with the enemy" as the old saying goes and the current state is a pay to play game with a pretty modest player base and lot of quite angry and vocal ex-players who are unhappy with the way things have played out.

I think there was an opportunity to right the ship with the move to Steam if the game had launched free to play with some gentle pricing to get the first few heroes. Unfortunately the path they took does not really seem to have worked out and yet another pivot is likely to piss off a bunch more people.

On top of this for one reason or another the game feels a bit stale to me as a long term player right now and the slower patching cycle is making this worse. I'm still playing a fair bit but nothing like I was and especially after the last balance was quite minor I am not playing much.

The exit of a few of the streamers also feels a bit bad and I suspect that is also linked to a reduction of available funds to keep them on board or just dropping engagement, again pure speculation.

Anyway, it is hard to see how the current player base and pricing approach could support even a modest permanent staff as well as the server infrastructure and other costs.

I don't have all the information but I still think if they moved to free to play with Stelle playable and then $5 for your first character unlock, $10 for the second and $20 from there on in you could potentially build the kind of large player base that this game was always designed around.

I disagree with you. I believe the Buy-to-Play model is a Lot more sustainable than the Free-to-Play one.

The F2P business model has three major problems:

The first problem is the playerbase distribution. Typically it is comprised of 80% of "freeloaders", who pay absolutely nothing (I don't mean that in a derogatory way), 15% of "minnows", who pay small amounts occasionally, and 5% of "whales", who pay large amounts and/or pay very regularly. At least 80%, probably 90% of the revenue the typical F2P game earns comes from "whales". So an F2P game needs to have a very large playerbase to be sustainable. "When the hype-train leaves the station", often as soon as a year after release, the game starts making losses. Soon after, it enters maintenance mode and eventually shuts down.

The second problem is, it is easy to register an account for an F2P game, but impossible to close it - the account just stays open indefinitely. So when Hearthstone claimed to have 40 million players (or some other such ridiculous number), they have simply counted the number of Registered Accounts, many of which were already "dead".

Thirdly, an F2P game needs a cash shop. And this cash shop can't just be cosmetic, or very few people would bother to buy anything from it. Eventually, players start complaining about Pay-to-Win and leave in droves. Especially if it becomes obvious that the dev team spend more time designing new cash shop items than anything gameplay related.

By comparison, the B2P model has 3 Advantages:

Firstly, it doesn't matter if a player gets bored and leaves after a month - they have already paid the minimum amount to sustain the game. And that amount can stay reasonable, because it's paid by everyone.

Secondly, no cash shop is needed. Most people, including myself, would much rather pay a small amount a couple times a year for genuinely new content than have to budget for new cosmetics that appear every month to tempt them to part with their cash again and again.

Thirdly, gamers have become much more savvy nowadays and realise that "Free" games often make them pay a lot more than simply buying the game normally. So F2P doesn't attract as much attention as it used to.

The F2P business model has three major problems:

The first problem is the playerbase distribution. Typically it is comprised of 80% of "freeloaders", who pay absolutely nothing (I don't mean that in a derogatory way), 15% of "minnows", who pay small amounts occasionally, and 5% of "whales", who pay large amounts and/or pay very regularly. At least 80%, probably 90% of the revenue the typical F2P game earns comes from "whales". So an F2P game needs to have a very large playerbase to be sustainable. "When the hype-train leaves the station", often as soon as a year after release, the game starts making losses. Soon after, it enters maintenance mode and eventually shuts down.

The second problem is, it is easy to register an account for an F2P game, but impossible to close it - the account just stays open indefinitely. So when Hearthstone claimed to have 40 million players (or some other such ridiculous number), they have simply counted the number of Registered Accounts, many of which were already "dead".

Thirdly, an F2P game needs a cash shop. And this cash shop can't just be cosmetic, or very few people would bother to buy anything from it. Eventually, players start complaining about Pay-to-Win and leave in droves. Especially if it becomes obvious that the dev team spend more time designing new cash shop items than anything gameplay related.

By comparison, the B2P model has 3 Advantages:

Firstly, it doesn't matter if a player gets bored and leaves after a month - they have already paid the minimum amount to sustain the game. And that amount can stay reasonable, because it's paid by everyone.

Secondly, no cash shop is needed. Most people, including myself, would much rather pay a small amount a couple times a year for genuinely new content than have to budget for new cosmetics that appear every month to tempt them to part with their cash again and again.

Thirdly, gamers have become much more savvy nowadays and realise that "Free" games often make them pay a lot more than simply buying the game normally. So F2P doesn't attract as much attention as it used to.

Typically it is comprised of 80% of "freeloaders", who pay absolutely nothing (I don't mean that in a derogatory way), 15% of "minnows", who pay small amounts occasionally, and 5% of "whales", who pay large amounts and/or pay very regularly. At least 80%, probably 90% of the revenue the typical F2P game earns comes from "whales". So an F2P game needs to have a very large playerbase to be sustainable. "When the hype-train leaves the station", often as soon as a year after release, the game starts making losses. Soon after, it enters maintenance mode and eventually shuts down.

The second problem is, it is easy to register an account for an F2P game, but impossible to close it - the account just stays open indefinitely. So when Hearthstone claimed to have 40 million players (or some other such ridiculous number), they have simply counted the number of Registered Accounts, many of which were already "dead".

Thirdly, an F2P game needs a cash shop. And this cash shop can't just be cosmetic, or very few people would bother to buy anything from it. Eventually, players start complaining about Pay-to-Win and leave in droves. Especially if it becomes obvious that the dev team spend more time designing new cash shop items than anything gameplay related.

By comparison, the B2P model has 3 Advantages:

Firstly, it doesn't matter if a player gets bored and leaves after a month - they have already paid the minimum amount to sustain the game. And that amount can stay reasonable, because it's paid by everyone.

Secondly, no cash shop is needed. Most people, including myself, would much rather pay a small amount a couple times a year for genuinely new content than have to budget for new cosmetics that appear every month to tempt them to part with their cash again and again.

Thirdly, gamers have become much more savvy nowadays and realise that "Free" games often make them pay a lot more than simply buying the game normally. So F2P doesn't attract as much attention as it used to.
